definition: The collection and monitoring of a device's or person's geographical position over time, typically through GPS, cellular towers, Wi-Fi networks, or other positioning technologies.
metaDescription: Learn about location tracking - how apps and services monitor your geographical position, privacy implications, and ways to protect your location data.
simpleExplanation: Location tracking is when your phone, apps, or online services keep track of where you are and where you go. This happens through GPS, cell towers, and Wi-Fi signals that can pinpoint your exact location and create a detailed map of your daily movements.
whyItMatters: Your location data reveals intimate details about your life - where you live, work, shop, and socialize. This information can be sold to advertisers, shared with governments, or used to infer personal details like your health conditions, political views, or relationships.
technicalDetail: Location tracking combines multiple data sources including GPS coordinates, cell tower triangulation, Wi-Fi access point mapping, and IP address geolocation. Apps can access this data through device APIs, while web services use IP addresses and browser geolocation features to determine approximate location.

examples.explanation: Apps like Google Maps track your location to provide turn-by-turn directions and estimate arrival times, but also build detailed profiles of your travel patterns and frequently visited places.
When you post photos or check-in at restaurants on social platforms, you're sharing your location data, which can be used to target ads or build location-based audience profiles.
Running apps track your routes and workout locations, potentially revealing sensitive information like your home address or daily exercise routine to the app company and their partners.
